quote: confidence, overconfidence, and underconfidence—being interpreted now
content:
Confidence has several dimensions
Moore and Healy distinguish estimates of one’s performance, placement relative to others and precision of belief. A person can be too pessimistic on one dimension while being too certain on another. The essay’s community-wide diagnosis needs measurements of those dimensions, not just memorable examples of modest people.
Moore & Healy (2008)

A few trials cannot rank your general potential
Trying a difficult task can reveal information that introspection misses. A handful of attempts still leaves substantial uncertainty and can be affected by task choice, practice and opponent strength. Treat the result as a local measurement with limits, not a reliable assessment of how high the person can ultimately rise.

quote: rationality is systematized winning and trying
content:
Choose a target that does not reward the wrong competence
A contest can supply concrete feedback, which is better than unmeasured self-assurance. Winning a debate may measure persuasion or opponent weakness more than truth; other challenges likewise reward their scoring rules. Choose an outcome linked to the capacity you want and keep calibration distinct from motivational confidence.

quote: I learned the first form of this
content:
Testing your own strategy survives; a universal first-instinct rule does not
Kruger and colleagues studied the first-instinct fallacy and the tendency to remember costly answer changes disproportionately. Their evidence cautions against a blanket rule to keep the first answer. The essay’s suggestion to examine one’s actual record is the sound component, provided that successes and failures are recorded prospectively.
Kruger, Wirtz & Miller (2005)
